title: JavaScript Foundations
description: Your first line of code starts here. Get comfortable with variables, decisions, and functions through clear, practical examples.

lessons.title: Variables & data types
lessons.intro: Think of a variable as a named container for a value. JavaScript lets you work with numbers, text, booleans, and more. A good variable name makes your code easier to understand.
lessons.body: Use const for values you will not reassign, and let for values that change. Strings go inside quotes; numbers and booleans do not. JavaScript infers the type from the value, so you do not need to declare it yourself.
lessons.takeaway: A const variable cannot be reassigned. A let variable can. Both have block scope, which means they belong to the block in which they are declared.
lessons.question: Which declaration should you use for a counter that changes?

lessons.title: Making decisions
lessons.intro: Programs become useful when they can make decisions. Conditional statements run different code depending on whether a condition evaluates to true or false.
lessons.body: Use if for a condition and else for the alternative. Comparison operators such as ===, >, and < produce booleans. Prefer === over == because it checks both the value and its type.
lessons.takeaway: Use && when both conditions must be true, || when either may be true, and ! to reverse a boolean.
lessons.question: What does 5 === '5' evaluate to?

lessons.title: Your first function
lessons.intro: A function is a reusable piece of logic. Give it inputs (parameters), let it do some work, and get a result back using return. This is the foundation of every CodeArena solution.
lessons.body: Declare a function with a descriptive name. Parameters act as local variables that receive arguments when you call it. Returning a value is different from logging it: our test runner checks returned values, not console output.
lessons.takeaway: A function without a return statement returns undefined. In coding challenges, return the answer so the tests can compare it with the expected result.
lessons.question: What does a function return when it has no return statement?

title: Arrays & Strings
description: Get hands-on with the building blocks of coding challenges. Store collections, iterate with purpose, and transform your data.

lessons.title: Working with arrays
lessons.intro: An array is an ordered collection of values. Think of it as a row of numbered boxes. The first box has index 0, the second index 1, and so on.
lessons.body: Use square brackets to access a value by index. The length property tells you how many values the array contains. push adds an item to the end, and pop removes the last item.
lessons.takeaway: Arrays are zero-indexed. The final valid index is array.length - 1. Accessing an index that does not exist returns undefined.
lessons.question: What is [10, 20, 30][1]?

lessons.title: Loops & iteration
lessons.intro: A loop repeats a block of code. Instead of writing a separate statement for each element, you can process arrays of any size with just a few lines.
lessons.body: A classic for loop has an initializer, a condition, and an update. Use for...of when you only need the values. Keep track of the boundaries: using < length avoids reading past the end.
lessons.takeaway: Check that your loop makes progress toward its stopping condition. A loop that never stops will hit the CodeArena execution time limit.
lessons.question: Which loop visits every valid array index?

lessons.title: Strings & transformations
lessons.intro: Strings are sequences of characters. You can read a character by index and use many built-in methods to transform text. Unlike arrays, JavaScript strings are immutable.
lessons.body: Use split to convert a string to an array, join to combine an array into a string, and toLowerCase to normalize text. Methods return new strings; they do not modify the original string.
lessons.takeaway: For basic lowercase English strings, sorting the characters gives a useful way to compare anagrams. For full Unicode text, character handling needs extra care.
lessons.question: Does toLowerCase() modify the original string?
options: No, it returns a new string

title: Think Like a Problem Solver
description: Learn to break down a challenge, choose the right data structure, and turn a working solution into a better one.

lessons.title: Understanding Big O
lessons.intro: Big O describes how an algorithm's work grows as its input gets larger. It helps you compare solutions without depending on a particular computer or exact running time.
lessons.body: Reading one array element is constant time, O(1). Visiting every element once is linear time, O(n). Comparing each element with every other element is typically quadratic, O(n²). Drop constants and lower-order terms when describing growth.
lessons.takeaway: Time complexity measures work; space complexity measures extra memory. A faster algorithm sometimes uses more space. Consider both.
lessons.question: What is the time complexity of visiting each element once?

lessons.title: The power of hash maps
lessons.intro: A Map stores key-value pairs. It is useful when you want to remember something you have already seen and look it up efficiently later.
lessons.concept: Trade a little space for speed
lessons.body: Use set to store a value, get to retrieve it, and has to check for a key. In practice, hash maps commonly provide average constant-time access; JavaScript requires average sublinear access. A map can replace a repeated search through an array.
lessons.takeaway: When a problem asks whether you have seen a value before, or how often it appears, consider using a Map or Set.
lessons.question: Which Map method checks whether a key exists?

lessons.title: Divide & conquer
lessons.intro: Sometimes you can make a problem smaller instead of checking everything. Binary search repeatedly discards half of a sorted search space.
lessons.concept: Half the work. Again and again.
lessons.body: Keep left and right boundaries. Compare the middle value with the target. If the target is larger, only the right half can contain it; otherwise, keep the left half. Continue until you find it or the boundaries cross.
lessons.takeaway: Binary search needs a sorted or otherwise monotonic search space. It takes O(log n) time and O(1) extra space in this iterative version.
lessons.question: What does binary search require?
